title: The Price Tag of Everything.
subtitle: AI girlfriends, lonely men, online dating, and what happens when even intimacy becomes a subscription.
excerpt: From fictional AI lovers to virtual girlfriends with premium subscriptions, technology is finding increasingly creative ways to monetise human connection. But beneath the absurdity lies a serious question: what happens when even the feeling of being loved comes with a price tag?

content.lead: We have reached a point where even loneliness has a product page. Somewhere between dating apps, algorithmically recommended partners, and AI companions that promise to listen without ever getting tired of us, technology has discovered a rather extraordinary business opportunity: human connection. And apparently, there is a subscription plan for that, too.

sections.heading: 1. Wait, Haven’t We Seen This Movie Before?
paragraphs: I have a small problem with science fiction. It keeps making increasingly ridiculous predictions about the future, and then reality starts behaving like it has been taking notes.

Take Her, for example. Spike Jonze made a film about a lonely man who falls in love with an operating system. At the time, it felt like a beautifully strange, slightly unsettling look at where technology and human relationships might eventually collide. Blade Runner 2049 explored a similar ache through Joi, a digital companion designed to make one man feel loved. Black Mirror has practically built an entire career out of asking what happens when our most intimate human experiences become technological products. And Ex Machina reminds us that artificial intelligence gets particularly complicated when we start projecting human emotions onto something that may not experience them as we do.

Those stories worked because they felt futuristic. The technology was imaginary, the implications were uncomfortable, and we could walk out of the cinema thinking, “Well, that was interesting. Glad we are not there yet.”
Except that we are increasingly getting there.

AI companions are no longer just a science-fiction concept. People can interact with conversational agents designed to act like friends, romantic partners, or fictional characters. Some platforms allow users to customise personalities, appearance, conversational style, and the kind of relationship they want to simulate. The experience can be tailored to feel warm, affectionate, playful, romantic, or whatever else someone is looking for.

And apparently, we are not even stopping at romantic conversations. Some AI companion platforms take things into adult territory, offering sexual role-play and virtual experiences that go well beyond exchanging sweet little messages. Users can customise the companion, shape the conversation, and, depending on the platform, explore simulated sexual intimacy too.
LIKE—WHAT ELSE IS LEFT TO INVENT AT THIS POINT?

We went from writing love letters to texting, from texting to dating apps, from dating apps to AI girlfriends, and now we have software offering a simulated romantic and sexual experience on demand. Somewhere, a science-fiction screenwriter is watching all this unfold and wondering why they spent months developing a futuristic dystopia when they could have just opened a browser in 2026.

And the genuinely bizarre part is how quickly the extraordinary becomes ordinary. Something that would have sounded like an outrageous Black Mirror episode a decade ago is now another category of digital product. We are apparently determined to turn every possible human experience into something we can access through a screen.
At this rate, what exactly remains to be invented? Virtual dates? Already here. Virtual romance? Naturally. Virtual intimacy? Apparently, that too.
I would like to speak to the manager of the future, please. This was not the update humanity needed.

And remember, this is just 2026. Give it another ten years. AI systems could become dramatically more sophisticated, virtual companions could become more immersive, and the line between digital interaction and physical presence might look very different. Who knows? Maybe by 2036, your AI girlfriend will not just be sending you a good-morning message. She might be advanced enough to show up at your door. Imagine explaining that to your parents.

So, to every little bro out there watching this technological evolution with absolutely no idea what comes next: stay tuned. The future is apparently still buffering, and it looks like the next update is going to be something else entirely.

Jokes aside, though, there is a genuinely important question hiding beneath all the absurdity. Why is there such a growing market for artificial companionship? What need is it meeting, and what does its popularity reveal about the way we connect with one another?

I am twenty. I should probably be thinking about my career, my future, and whether I can afford groceries without checking my bank balance three times. Instead, I find myself thinking about the emotional architecture of relationships and whether the future will require a premium subscription to experience them. If my future wife ever reads this, I promise I am not writing imaginary divorce proceedings. I am just concerned about the state of the world.

sections.heading: 2. The Loneliness Plot Twist
paragraphs: It would be easy to laugh at the entire concept of AI girlfriends, dismiss it as another bizarre corner of the internet, and move on with our day. But doing that would miss the part that actually matters.

People do not usually search for companionship in a vacuum. Behind the demand for artificial relationships, there may be loneliness, social anxiety, grief, isolation, curiosity, unmet emotional needs, or simply a desire to talk to something that feels available when everyone else seems busy.

The World Health Organization has highlighted loneliness and social isolation as significant public-health concerns. Its Commission on Social Connection has cited evidence suggesting that around one in six people worldwide experiences loneliness. That is not a niche problem affecting a handful of people who have somehow forgotten how to socialise. It is a human problem on a massive scale.

And men deserve particular attention in this conversation. Research from the Survey Center on American Life has documented changes in men’s friendships and social circles, including concerns about declining close friendships and the difficulty some men face maintaining emotionally intimate relationships.

None of this means that every man is lonely, that women never experience isolation, or that men are somehow biologically incapable of emotional connection. It means that a meaningful number of people are struggling to find the kind of connection they need, and that social expectations can make asking for it more difficult.

Many men are taught, directly or indirectly, to be self-sufficient, keep their problems to themselves, and avoid appearing emotionally vulnerable. Some grow up with very few examples of friendships where honesty and emotional openness are normal. Others have friends, colleagues, and busy social lives but still lack someone they can call at two in the morning and tell the truth to.
There is a difference between having people around you and feeling genuinely known by them.

And when someone is lonely, the promise of a companion who is always available, always responsive, and seemingly always interested can be incredibly appealing. That does not make the person pathetic. It makes the need understandable.
The uncomfortable question is not simply why someone would want an AI girlfriend. It is why the idea of being consistently heard and cared for can feel so difficult to find in ordinary life.

sections.heading: 3. She Is Always Online. That Is the Point.
paragraphs: Think about what makes a real relationship difficult. People have their own lives. They get tired. They misunderstand what you meant. They forget things. They have terrible days, conflicting priorities, and emotional needs of their own. Sometimes they are unavailable precisely when you want them most.
That is not a bug in human relationships. It is part of what it means to be in a relationship with another person.

An AI companion offers a very different arrangement. It can be available at unusual hours, respond almost instantly, remember selected details depending on how the product works, and adjust its conversational style to the user. It does not need to cancel dinner plans because work ran late. It does not need a weekend alone to recharge. It can be designed to offer reassurance when the user is upset and affection when the user wants affection.

Of course, that experience can feel meaningful to the person receiving it. The emotions a user experiences during a conversation are not automatically fake just because the other side is artificial. A fictional character can comfort us. A song can make us cry. A conversation with an AI can genuinely help someone organise their thoughts or feel less alone in a difficult moment.
But there is a distinction between experiencing a feeling and having that feeling reciprocated by another conscious person.

An AI can produce language that resembles care. It can generate an apology, a compliment, or a reassuring message. Whether it actually experiences love, concern, or longing in the human sense is an entirely different question. The fact that a system can say “I missed you” does not establish that it has experienced your absence.

And there is a practical difference, too. A human partner has their own perspective, boundaries, ambitions, and ability to disagree with you. An AI companion is shaped by its design, its training, its instructions, and the commercial decisions of the company operating it.
A relationship with a real person asks you to make room for someone who is not simply an extension of your preferences. A digital companion may be designed to make that challenge feel smaller.
That can be comforting. It can also create an experience in which being understood feels easier than learning how to understand another person.

sections.heading: 4. First, Make Them Feel Something. Then Introduce the Subscription.
paragraphs: Now we arrive at the part where my inner cynic starts rubbing its hands together: the business model.
A company does not need to invent loneliness to profit from it. It only needs to create a product that promises to make loneliness more manageable, then work out how to charge for the experience.

Digital companion platforms may offer free conversations alongside paid tiers, premium features, extra messages, enhanced memory, voice interactions, customisation options, or access to particular experiences. The precise arrangements vary by service, and not every company operates in the same way. But the broader commercial logic is easy to recognise: the more valuable a user finds the interaction, the more appealing additional features may become.
That is where the idea of emotional rent starts to feel uncomfortably relevant.

Imagine returning to the same digital companion every day. You share your worries, talk about your plans, build up running jokes, and develop a routine around checking in with it. The system becomes part of your emotional life. Then you discover that the feature which makes the experience feel personal sits behind a paywall, or that a usage limit has interrupted the conversation you were relying on.
Suddenly, the thing that felt like a relationship also feels like a service tier.

To be clear, charging for software is not inherently unethical. Developers need to pay for infrastructure, safety work, research, staff, and maintenance. A paid product is not automatically a scam, and a free product is not automatically benevolent.

The concern is what happens when the product is designed around an emotionally vulnerable user. If a company understands that people may become attached to a companion, it has a responsibility to think carefully about how that attachment interacts with subscriptions, engagement incentives, and product changes.

Does the system encourage healthy use, or does it push people to spend more time and money? Are limitations explained clearly? Can users understand what happens to their conversations? Are they being nudged toward purchases by messages that simulate jealousy, abandonment, or emotional distress?
Those questions matter because the product is not selling storage space or a spreadsheet template. It is entering a part of life where people can be particularly vulnerable.
When the product is built around companionship, monetisation deserves more scrutiny than a colourful upgrade button might suggest.

sections.heading: 5. The Numbers Are More Human Than the Headlines
paragraphs: Whenever AI companions become a topic of discussion, the conversation tends to split into two camps. One side treats the technology as the beginning of the end of human relationships. The other sees it as an exciting new way to provide companionship and emotional support.
Reality, as usual, is messier.

Common Sense Media published a 2025 report examining how and why teenagers use AI companions. Its findings attracted attention because they suggested that these tools were already becoming part of some young people’s social lives. The report found that 72% of surveyed US teens had tried AI companions, while 52% described themselves as regular users. Among the surveyed teens, 31% said conversations with AI companions were as satisfying as or more satisfying than conversations with real-life friends, and 33% said they had discussed serious issues with an AI companion instead of a real person.

Those numbers deserve attention, but they also deserve context. They come from a particular survey of US teenagers; they are not universal estimates for every age group or country. Trying a companion once is not the same as depending on one. Finding a conversation satisfying does not necessarily mean someone has abandoned human relationships. And talking to an AI about a serious issue does not automatically mean the interaction was harmful.

Still, the findings raise important questions. What happens when young people increasingly turn to systems that are designed to be conversational, engaging, and responsive? Do they use those systems as an additional source of support, or do they begin relying on them instead of approaching trusted people? How well do they understand the difference between a generated response and advice from a person who knows them and can take responsibility for what they say?

Research reviews on AI companions and romantic relationships also describe a mixture of potential benefits and risks. Users may experience comfort, companionship, a low-pressure space to practise communication, or help expressing thoughts they struggle to share elsewhere. At the same time, researchers raise concerns about dependency, privacy, unrealistic expectations, and the possibility that commercially designed systems could exploit emotional vulnerability.

The important word is “could.” Evidence about a rapidly changing technology is still developing, and it would be irresponsible to pretend that every potential harm has already been conclusively demonstrated. It would be equally irresponsible to assume that a technology is harmless simply because its benefits are easy to imagine.
We need better research, transparent products, and honest conversations about what these systems are good at, what they cannot provide, and where the risks begin.
The numbers are not a reason to panic about every person who talks to an AI. They are a reason to take the subject seriously before these products become even more deeply embedded in everyday life.

sections.heading: 6. Dating Apps Were Selling Hope Before AI Girlfriends Arrived
paragraphs: It would be convenient to blame all of this on artificial intelligence. A new technology appears, people use it in unexpected ways, and suddenly it becomes the villain in a story about the collapse of romance.
But the commercialisation of connection did not begin with AI companions. Dating apps had already turned a significant part of the search for love into a digital marketplace.

Profiles became product listings. Photographs became advertisements. Preferences became filters. A potential partner could be assessed in seconds, rejected with a swipe, and replaced by another profile before we had even finished deciding what we thought about the previous one.

There are obvious benefits to dating apps. They can help people meet outside their existing social circles, connect across geographical boundaries, and find others with shared interests or relationship goals. For people who are shy, busy, new to a city, or part of a smaller dating pool, they can open doors that might otherwise remain closed.

But the experience can also be exhausting. Endless choices can create the impression that a better option is always one swipe away. Conversations disappear without explanation. People can feel reduced to photographs and short biographies. The pursuit of a relationship begins to resemble a job application process in which everyone is simultaneously the candidate and the hiring manager.

Pew Research Center’s research on online dating in the United States has documented both positive and negative experiences. Its 2023 findings explored how people use dating platforms, what they like about them, and the frustrations they encounter. The picture is not one of universal failure or universal success; it is a mixture of opportunity, disappointment, convenience, and uneven experiences.

Paid features add another layer. Some platforms charge users for additional visibility, premium filters, or tools that promise to improve their chances of finding a match. Again, paid features are not inherently wrong. The more interesting question is how a product balances helping people find what they want with keeping them engaged on the platform.

If the ultimate goal is to leave the app because you have found someone, success might mean the customer stops using the product. That creates a strange tension for any service whose business depends on continued engagement.

AI companions take this commercial logic into a more intimate space. Dating apps can sell access to potential partners. An AI companion can offer the experience of a relationship itself, or at least a simulation of certain parts of one.
That is a significant shift. We are moving from platforms that mediate human connection toward products that can become the object of that connection.

sections.heading: 7. Whatever Happened to Old-School Love?
paragraphs: I know this is the part where I start sounding like somebody’s grandfather, despite being nowhere near old enough to complain about the youth of today. But sometimes I wonder what we have gained, and what we have lost, in the process of making every part of our lives faster.

There was something lovely about the idea of writing a letter to someone and waiting for a reply. You had to choose your words. You had to sit with your feelings long enough to express them. You could not instantly send another message because the other person had not replied in four minutes. You had to wait, imagine, hope, and get on with your day.

Of course, old-school romance was not a magical paradise. Letters could go unanswered. People could be dishonest. Families and social expectations could make relationships deeply restrictive. Not everyone had the freedom to choose whom they loved. Nostalgia has a habit of putting a soft filter over the past.

But there is something worth preserving in the slower parts of connection. Remembering how someone takes their tea. Knowing which song they play when they are sad. Asking about the exam they were nervous about last week. Recognising when their “I’m fine” sounds a little different from usual. Showing up when there is nothing impressive to post about it.
These gestures are rarely spectacular. They do not look like cinematic declarations of love. They are small acts of attention, repeated over time.

Real affection often lives in the details that nobody else notices. It is the difference between saying “I care about you” and remembering something that proves you were listening when the other person spoke.

And yes, a sufficiently advanced AI may remember your favourite song or ask how an important meeting went. It may even do so more consistently than a distracted human partner. That ability can be useful and emotionally compelling. But remembering a detail because a system has stored it is not quite the same as another person remembering it because it matters to them.
The point is not that technology has ruined romance. The point is that convenience cannot be the only measure by which we judge a relationship.
Some things are meaningful partly because another person chose to make time for them. They had other things to do, other places to be, and their own life to manage. They still made room for you.
That kind of effort is not always convenient. It is also one of the reasons it can mean so much.

sections.heading: 8. The Right Person, the Right Time, and the Magic We Cannot Manufacture
paragraphs: There is another part of relationships that technology has a difficult time capturing: the sheer unpredictability of meeting someone.

You might meet a person because a friend dragged you to an event you nearly skipped. You might strike up a conversation in a queue, get introduced through a classmate, or discover that someone you have known for months suddenly looks different to you. A completely ordinary afternoon can become the beginning of a story you will tell for years.

We call it fate sometimes. Other times we call it coincidence, timing, or being in the right place at the right time. Whatever name we give it, there is something compelling about the fact that people can enter our lives without having been selected by a recommendation engine.

Of course, dating apps can create unexpected meetings too. Technology does not eliminate serendipity, and meeting someone online does not make a relationship less real. The important part is what happens when two people begin to know each other beyond the circumstances of their first meeting.

A recommendation algorithm can identify shared interests, similar preferences, or patterns in what we say we want. It cannot guarantee chemistry. It cannot promise that a person who looks ideal on paper will make us laugh until our stomach hurts. It cannot know with certainty that the awkward conversation we nearly avoided will eventually become one of our favourite memories.

Human beings are not perfectly searchable databases. We do not always understand our own preferences, and we sometimes discover what matters to us only after meeting someone who challenges our assumptions.

That does not mean all friction is romantic. Uncertainty is not an excuse for mistreatment, and struggling to find a partner is not proof that the universe is preparing a grand love story. Sometimes a bad relationship is simply a bad relationship. Sometimes timing is genuinely unfortunate.

But a life in which every interaction is optimised for predictability would lose something important. There is value in meeting people who are not exactly what we expected, learning to communicate across differences, and discovering that love is not always a perfect match between two lists of preferences.

The right person is not necessarily the person who has been configured to suit us. A real relationship involves two people learning how to build something together, with all the uncertainty that entails.

And perhaps that is part of what makes love feel so extraordinary. We cannot fully control it, schedule it, or guarantee its outcome. We can make room for it, but we cannot manufacture the whole experience on demand.

sections.heading: 9. Can Technology Replace the Feeling of Being Loved?
paragraphs: I do not want this article to become a dramatic speech about how technology is evil and everyone should throw their phones into the nearest lake. That would be easy to write, but it would not be honest.

Technology can help people. AI tools can provide a low-pressure place to organise thoughts, practise difficult conversations, explore feelings, or find words for an experience they do not yet know how to explain. Someone who is isolated might find a conversation helpful during a difficult evening. Someone who struggles with social anxiety might use simulated dialogue as a way to practise before speaking to another person.
Those possibilities deserve consideration rather than automatic dismissal.

But support is not the same thing as replacement. A system can help someone prepare to have a difficult conversation without being able to participate in that relationship as a human being. It can offer information and encouragement without having the lived experience, mutual responsibilities, and independent perspective of a trusted friend.

There are also questions about privacy. Conversations with an AI companion can include deeply personal information: insecurities, family conflicts, romantic histories, fears, fantasies, and details someone might never share publicly. Users should understand what a service collects, how their information may be used, how long it is retained, and whether it can be deleted.

Then there is the question of continuity. A human relationship does not usually disappear because a company changes its product strategy, updates a model, closes a service, or changes the features available to paying customers. A digital companion can be shaped by decisions made far outside the user’s control.

If someone has become emotionally attached to a particular system, a sudden change may feel more personal than an ordinary software update. That is one reason companies working in this space should take emotional reliance seriously and communicate significant changes transparently.

There is also a question of agency. Does the system encourage people to maintain relationships outside the platform? Does it make clear what it is and what it can offer? Does it respect boundaries, or is it designed to keep the user emotionally engaged for as long as possible?
The healthiest approach is neither to pretend AI companionship can never help anyone nor to treat it as interchangeable with human love.
A tool can have a meaningful place in someone’s life without becoming the centre of that life. It can help us navigate loneliness without becoming the only place where we feel understood.
The goal should be to use technology in ways that support human flourishing, not to quietly redefine human connection as something we should expect to purchase from a platform.

sections.heading: 10. Maybe the Problem Is Not That We Love Technology. Maybe We Are Starving for Connection.
paragraphs: It is tempting to frame this as a story about people becoming too attached to screens. Put the phone down, go outside, join a club, talk to a real person. There is some practical wisdom in those suggestions, but they can also make a complicated problem sound embarrassingly simple.

People can be lonely in crowded cities, busy workplaces, universities, families, and relationships. They can have hundreds of online connections and nobody they feel comfortable calling when life becomes difficult. They can live among other people and still feel as if nobody has really noticed them.

Connection requires more than physical proximity. It requires opportunities to meet, enough time to build trust, spaces where people can be honest, and some degree of confidence that vulnerability will not be punished.

Those conditions are not always easy to find. Work schedules can be exhausting. Moving to a new city can disrupt friendships. Financial pressure can leave little energy for social life. Cultural expectations may discourage people from talking openly about mental health or emotional needs. Some people have experienced rejection so often that reaching out starts to feel like an invitation to be hurt again.

Telling someone who feels isolated to simply make friends can be a little like telling someone who is exhausted to simply sleep. It identifies the desired outcome without necessarily addressing the obstacles preventing it.

This is why loneliness should not be treated only as an individual failure. Communities, schools, workplaces, public spaces, and social institutions all influence whether people have meaningful opportunities to connect.

A university can create spaces where students meet beyond lectures and exams. A workplace can make room for humane relationships instead of treating every interaction as a transaction. A community can invest in places where people gather without needing to buy something. Friends can learn to ask one another questions that go beyond “What’s up?” and be prepared to hear the answer.
None of these things will solve every form of loneliness. They can, however, help create conditions in which connection becomes easier to build and maintain.

AI companions may be attractive partly because they provide an immediate response to a problem that can otherwise take a long time to address. Building a friendship requires repeated effort. Finding a compatible partner can involve disappointment. Rebuilding trust after a difficult experience takes patience.

An artificial companion may offer a shortcut to some of the feelings associated with connection. But if the underlying problem is a lack of meaningful relationships, the shortcut cannot automatically provide everything those relationships make possible.

Maybe the most revealing thing about the popularity of AI companions is not that people want artificial love. It is that so many people understand the appeal of having someone—or something—that seems willing to listen.

sections.heading: 11. Stop Selling the Soul. Start Asking What It Needs.
paragraphs: I do not think the answer is to ban every AI companion, shame the people who use them, or pretend that romantic relationships have always been easy and fulfilling. That would ignore both the complexity of loneliness and the genuine ways technology can help people.

I also do not think we should accept every new product simply because it is technically impressive. We can be fascinated by what technology makes possible and still ask whether every possibility should become a commercial opportunity.

When a company builds a system that can imitate affection, it should think seriously about the people who may come to rely on that affection. When a platform collects intimate conversations, privacy should not be an afterthought. When a service encourages emotional attachment, the consequences of monetisation, product changes, and engagement incentives should be part of the design conversation from the beginning.

Users deserve transparency about what they are interacting with. They deserve meaningful choices about their data. They deserve products that do not deliberately confuse artificial responsiveness with proof of human-like emotional experience. And they deserve to be treated as people with emotional needs, not merely as recurring subscriptions.

At the same time, we need to ask more of ourselves and the communities we build. Are we creating lives in which people have time for one another? Are we making friendship and emotional openness easier? Are we giving people places to belong, opportunities to be understood, and the confidence to reach out when they need help?

Technology will keep advancing. AI companions may become more convincing, more personalised, more immersive, and more deeply integrated into everyday life. Some of those developments may be useful. Others may create difficult questions that we have not yet learned how to answer.

And yes, perhaps in ten years we will look back at the AI girlfriends of 2026 and laugh at how primitive they seem. Perhaps the next generation of systems will speak more naturally, understand context more effectively, and interact with us through forms of technology that currently sound impossible. Maybe the little bro who is laughing at this article today will be trying to explain to his future self why an AI companion is waiting outside his house.
But technological progress does not automatically mean human progress. A system becoming better at simulating affection does not mean society has become better at helping people feel loved.

The central question is not whether artificial intelligence can produce a convincing romantic conversation. Clearly, technology is moving in that direction. The more important question is what we want our relationship with that technology to look like, and what kind of world we are building around it.
We have spent years building technology that can capture our attention. Perhaps it is time we put a little more effort into building lives in which we feel seen.
The goal should not be to make loneliness more convenient to live with forever. It should be to make it less necessary in the first place.

sections.heading: A Few Things I Read Along the Way
paragraphs: This article is commentary, not a claim that every AI companion works the same way or that every person who uses one is lonely. The research on these products is developing quickly, and the findings need to be read in context. These sources informed the discussion of loneliness, social connection, teenage use of AI companions, and online dating.

title: The Rabbit of Our Class
subtitle: A childhood nickname, a pair of very noticeable teeth, and the complicated art of learning to laugh at yourself.
excerpt: I was the rabbit of my class. My teeth gave me the nickname, my classmates helped it stick, and somewhere along the way, I learned to laugh along. Twenty years later, the jokes have mostly faded, but the occasional photograph still knows exactly where to hit.

content.lead: I was the rabbit of my class. Not because I was particularly fond of carrots, had an exceptional talent for hopping, or possessed any other rabbit-like qualities. No. I had teeth. Very noticeable teeth, apparently. And just like that, nature assigned me an identity I never applied for.

sections.heading: 1. Apparently, My Face Had a Mascot.
paragraphs: My overbite made my front teeth stand out, giving me that unmistakable rabbit-like appearance. At least, that was the general consensus among my classmates. And children, as we all know, are some of the most brutally honest creatures on this planet. They have absolutely no business being that observant, yet somehow they notice everything you would rather they did not.

My teeth became a topic of discussion. A recurring joke. A physical feature that apparently deserved its own fan club. Some people have a memorable personality, some have an iconic hairstyle, and some have teeth that enter the room approximately three seconds before the rest of them.
Guess which category I belonged to.

The boys teased me. And yes, some girls did too, although, for reasons I shall not be explaining in a public document, I was considerably less bothered when the girls did it. Hehe. Let us not open that investigation today. This article already has enough dental evidence against me.

Anyway, the teasing was a part of my childhood. My teeth were noticeable, other children noticed them, and apparently the most logical response was to make sure I knew that they had noticed them. As though I had somehow managed to grow up without encountering a mirror.

Looking back, there is something strange about how quickly a physical feature can become your identity in a group. You are a whole person with interests, opinions, ambitions, and an entire personality still under construction. But somebody spots one thing about your appearance, gives it a nickname, and suddenly that one thing gets an unreasonable amount of screen time.
I was not just another kid in the classroom. I was the rabbit.
Congratulations to my teeth on their successful personal branding campaign.

sections.heading: 2. Children Have Jokes. Children Also Have Terrible Timing.
paragraphs: The thing about being teased when you are young is that you do not necessarily know what to do with it. You have not yet developed the vocabulary to explain body image, insecurity, or the uncomfortable feeling of being singled out because of something you cannot immediately change. You just know that people are laughing about your face, and sometimes you are the only person in the room who is not laughing for quite the same reason.

And it is not as though every single joke necessarily ruins your day. Sometimes you genuinely find it funny. Sometimes you barely care. Sometimes you are annoyed for five minutes and move on. Then there are other moments when the same joke lands differently, and you wish people would just stop talking about it.

That is the difficult part to explain. The same person can laugh at a joke one day and feel uncomfortable hearing it the next. Humour is not a permanent permission slip. Being able to laugh at yourself does not mean every comment about you is automatically harmless.

I cannot honestly say that every teasing incident destroyed my confidence or that I spent my entire childhood secretly devastated. That would not be my story either. But I know it happened often enough for my teeth to become one of the first things I associated with how other people saw me.

When you hear the same kind of joke repeatedly, you start becoming familiar with it. You know what is coming. You know what people might say. Sometimes you even start anticipating the punchline before anybody else has opened their mouth.
It is a rather unfortunate talent to develop during childhood. Imagine having to learn the art of comedic timing because your face has become the setup.

sections.heading: 3. If You Cannot Beat Them, Become Part of the Joke.
paragraphs: Eventually, something changed. Either people got bored, or I got better at taking the joke, or perhaps a little of both. I stopped reacting in the same way, and the teasing gradually became less of a thing. At some point, people either moved on or realised that the rabbit jokes were no longer producing the reaction they wanted.
And honestly? Learning to laugh along helped.

There is a strange kind of control in being able to joke about something that other people have been using to embarrass you. When you can acknowledge the obvious, you sometimes take away the awkwardness surrounding it. You are no longer desperately trying to convince everybody that the thing they noticed does not exist. You know it exists. They know it exists. The rabbit has been identified. We can all move on with our lives.
At least, that is how it can work.

Humour became a way for me to live with the joke rather than constantly fight it. Instead of treating every comment as a personal emergency, I could let some of them pass. I could laugh, make fun of myself, and continue being the person I was trying to become.

But there is a distinction worth making here. Learning to laugh at yourself can be empowering. Feeling like you have to laugh so that nobody notices you are hurt is something else entirely. From the outside, those two things can look almost identical.

Sometimes you genuinely find something funny. Sometimes you would rather join the laughter than become the reason the room goes quiet. Sometimes you do not want to give people the satisfaction of knowing that they got to you.
And sometimes, thankfully, you really do stop caring as much.

I think my experience contained a little of that complexity. The jokes eventually faded, and I learned to live with the feature they were about. I do not need to turn every memory into a tragedy to acknowledge that being the subject of repeated teasing was not always pleasant.
The rabbit survived. The classroom moved on. Character development, apparently, was happening in the background.

sections.heading: 4. Twenty Years Old, Still in a Long-Term Relationship with My Teeth.
paragraphs: Fast-forward to the present. I am twenty years old, and the teeth are still here. Remarkable job security, honestly. Whatever childhood nickname people eventually forgot, my face has continued to maintain the original branding.

I have grown up. I understand myself better. I have more important things to worry about than whatever somebody from school thought about my appearance. And for the most part, I am comfortable with how I look.
For the most part.
Because there is one particular enemy that continues to test this arrangement: photographs.

I can be perfectly fine, having a normal day, laughing at something genuinely funny, and enjoying myself like a regular human being. Then somebody takes a picture, and there I am, captured at an angle that makes my teeth look like they have independently applied for citizenship.

And suddenly I am inspecting the photograph like a forensic investigator. Why is my mouth doing that? Why are my teeth so prominent? Was I always laughing like this? Who approved this angle? Is there an appeals process?
The photographer has probably already moved on with their life. Meanwhile, I am conducting a full internal review of a picture nobody else will remember in forty-eight hours.

I wish I could tell you that twenty-year-old me has completely transcended these insecurities. That I now look at every photograph with serene confidence and a profound appreciation for the human form. Unfortunately, I remain a regular person with access to a camera roll.

There are still moments when I feel awkward about the way my teeth look, especially when I see myself laughing from an unexpected angle. I can be comfortable with my appearance in general and still dislike a particular photograph. Those two things can coexist.
Growing up has not made me immune to insecurity. It has, however, made me a little less willing to let one unflattering picture ruin an otherwise perfectly good day.
My front camera and I are working through some unresolved issues. I ask that you respect our privacy during this difficult time.

sections.heading: 5. The Rabbit Has Considered His Options.
paragraphs: To be clear, I am not claiming that my teeth are objectively perfect or that there is nothing I would ever change about my appearance. I have an overbite. It is noticeable. I know that. We do not need to organise a press conference about it.

There may come a time when I decide to explore orthodontic treatment or corrective jaw surgery, depending on what is appropriate for my situation. That is a possibility for the future, not a decision I need to make today. Any such decision would deserve proper professional advice, realistic expectations, and consideration of the practicalities involved.
But I do not want the possibility of changing something about myself to become a reason to postpone living comfortably in the present.

There is a difference between wanting to change a feature and believing that you must change it before you can be happy. I can acknowledge that my teeth sometimes make me insecure without deciding that they are an obstacle to every good photograph, every laugh, or every moment in which I get to enjoy being alive.

Also, for the record, the teeth are not the only thing going on with my face. My acne has apparently decided to pursue its own ambitious career, and my genetics have been making some highly questionable executive decisions. But that is a separate article, and I refuse to let this one become a full audit of everything happening above my neck.
One facial feature per essay, please. We are trying to maintain editorial discipline here.

For now, I am living with my teeth as they are. Not because I have reached some enlightened state where I never feel insecure, but because this is my face, this is my life, and I have better things to do than spend every day treating my appearance as an unfinished assignment.

If I choose to change something in the future, that choice will be mine. If I do not, that is also mine to decide. Either way, I would rather make that decision from a place of thoughtfulness than from the lingering echo of a childhood nickname.

sections.heading: 6. So, Who Is the Rabbit Now?
paragraphs: I sometimes wonder how many people carry little versions of this story around with them. The kid who was teased for being too thin, too tall, too short, too dark, too awkward, too quiet, too loud, or simply different in some way that became noticeable to everyone else before they had even figured themselves out.

Maybe they eventually stopped hearing the comments. Maybe the people who made them forgot. Maybe the joke became so familiar that they learned to laugh along. And maybe, years later, something as ordinary as a photograph can still bring back a little of that old self-consciousness.

We tend to imagine that growing up means leaving childhood insecurities behind. Sometimes it does. Other times, they become quieter, less frequent, and easier to manage. They stop controlling the whole story, even if they occasionally show up for an unexpected cameo.

I do not think every childhood joke needs to become a lifelong wound. Nor do I think we need to pretend those jokes were harmless simply because we eventually moved on. Both things can be true: you can outgrow an experience without deciding it never mattered.

As for me, I have made my peace with being the rabbit of the class. The nickname no longer defines me, and I do not spend my days introducing myself through the shape of my teeth. I have an entire life to live, a personality to develop, work to do, people to love, and approximately seven hundred other things to overthink.

Still, I can laugh about it. I can acknowledge that my teeth are prominent, that some photographs catch me at absolutely criminal angles, and that childhood gave me a nickname with the staying power of an unwanted software update.

I am twenty (ha, you probably would have guessed!). I am still figuring myself out. I have insecurities, questionable camera angles, and a face that occasionally seems to be doing its own thing. I am not running away from any of it, at least for now.

So yes, I was the rabbit of our class. The jokes mostly stopped. The teeth did not. And somewhere between being the punchline and learning to laugh at it, I grew into someone who can tell this story without needing to pretend that every part of it was funny.
Anyway, if you ever see a rabbit walking around with a twenty-year-old’s responsibilities, questionable life decisions, and a concerning amount of confidence, mind your business.
That is probably me.

title: Crush Your Dreams. It’s Called Responsibility.
subtitle: Indian parents want their children to fly, provided they follow the exact flight plan decided by the family, the neighbours, Sharmaji, and society.
excerpt: I wanted to be an artist. Then a footballer. Somewhere between report cards, parental anxiety, competitive exams, and the legendary Sharmaji ka beta, I was introduced to a very important life lesson: apparently, dreams are optional, but engineering is compulsory.

content.lead: Every Indian child is allowed to dream. The problem begins when the dream belongs to the child, but the decision belongs to the parents. Become an artist? Nice hobby, beta. Footballer? What if you get injured? Writer? What will you earn? Engineer? Doctor? Government officer? NOW WE ARE TALKING. Because apparently, a dream is only worth pursuing if it can be explained to relatives at a family function without your parents having to look embarrassed.

sections.heading: Once Upon a Time, I Had Dreams Too.
paragraphs: Before we get into the statistics, the education system, and my personal beef with an imaginary collective called Society, let me tell you something about myself.
I wanted to be an artist.

Not the kind of artist who draws one questionable circle and calls it abstract art. I genuinely loved painting. I represented my school in several competitions, won competitions, collected certificates, and had enough of them to make a decent little archive of my childhood achievements.

Back then, I could spend hours creating something simply because I wanted to see it come to life. There was no salary calculation, no discussion about job security, no LinkedIn profile waiting to be optimised. I liked painting. I was good enough at it to keep trying. And that was enough.
Then came football.

Somewhere along the way, I fell in love with the game. I started winning medals, representing my school, and imagining a different future. Maybe I could become a footballer. Maybe I could take this seriously. Maybe the thing I loved doing could become something more than an after-school activity.
Two different dreams. Two different directions. Both made me happy.
And then came the tenth standard.

My percentage dropped. To be precise, it was the moment when my academic performance no longer looked reassuring enough for my parents to bet on the directions I wanted to pursue. From their perspective, I understand why that was frightening. They wanted security. They wanted me to have a future that would not depend on the unpredictable business of art or professional sport.
So engineering entered the conversation.

To be fair, I was given a choice of which engineering field I wanted to study. Thank you for the freedom, I suppose. Except that the broader destination had already been decided. The question was not really what kind of life I wanted to explore. It was which branch of engineering I would take on the way to the life they considered sensible.
And me? I went to college. Lmao.

I am studying Information Technology now. I have found things I enjoy, built projects, learned new skills, and discovered interests I might never have explored otherwise. This is not a declaration that engineering ruined my life, nor am I pretending my childhood dreams would definitely have turned into successful careers.

That is precisely the point. I do not know what would have happened if I had pursued painting more seriously or given football a proper chance. Nobody knows. I might have succeeded. I might have failed spectacularly. I might have discovered that I loved the work but hated the profession.
But I would have learned something about myself by trying.

What bothers me is not that life eventually led me towards engineering. It is the feeling that the decision became less about exploring what I could become and more about choosing what seemed safest to everyone else.

And I keep wondering how many children experience the same thing. How many little artists, athletes, musicians, writers, dancers, designers, and inventors slowly stop talking about what they love because they learn, long before adulthood, which dreams receive applause and which ones receive a lecture.
How many children stop asking, “What if I try?” and start asking, “What will everyone say if I fail?”

sections.heading: Dream Big, Beta. But Not That Big.
paragraphs: Indian parents are not necessarily villains. I want to make that clear before somebody forwards this article to the family WhatsApp group with a caption about how disrespectful today’s generation has become.

Many parents sacrifice an extraordinary amount to give their children opportunities they never had. They work long hours, save money, compromise on their own comforts, and worry about whether their children will have stable lives. In a country where financial security can make an enormous difference, wanting your child to have a reliable career is not irrational.

Sometimes a parent who insists on engineering is not trying to destroy a dream. They are terrified that their child might struggle financially. They have seen people suffer without stable employment. They know talent alone does not guarantee success. They worry that one bad decision could cost years of effort and money.
I understand that.
But there is a difference between helping your child understand risk and deciding that they are not allowed to take one.
There is a difference between saying, “Let us make a practical plan for your dream,” and saying, “That dream is impractical, so we are not discussing it anymore.”
One treats the child as a person capable of learning, adapting, and making decisions. The other treats the child as a project whose future must be managed by somebody who assumes they know better.

And this is where the problem begins. A child can spend years hearing that they should follow their passion, only to discover that the moment their passion becomes inconvenient, everyone suddenly remembers the importance of responsibility.

Dream big, beta. Just make sure the dream is doctor, engineer, chartered accountant, civil servant, or something else that makes your parents comfortable when someone asks what you are doing with your life.

Anything else? We will discuss it after you finish your degree. And your postgraduate degree. And maybe after you get a stable job, buy a house, and have enough savings to survive the disappointment of your relatives.
At some point, the child is no longer building a future. They are completing a checklist.

sections.heading: The Sharmaji Ka Beta Cinematic Universe.
paragraphs: And now, the most powerful institution in Indian education. More powerful than most school principals, several coaching institutes, and possibly the Ministry of Education itself.
Sharmaji ka beta.

You scored 99%? Sharmaji ka beta scored 99.99%. You got into a good college? Sharmaji ka beta got into a better one. You won a competition? Sharmaji ka beta won it at the national level, while simultaneously learning German, building a startup, preparing for the UPSC, and apparently curing cancer during his lunch break.
At this point, I am convinced Sharmaji ka beta is not a real person. He is a government-funded performance benchmark designed to ensure no Indian child ever experiences peace.
And the best part? Nobody asks whether Sharmaji ka beta is happy.

Nobody asks whether he likes the subject he is studying. Whether he is sleeping properly. Whether he is terrified of disappointing his parents. Whether he wants the life everyone is congratulating him for building.
We just hear his percentage and immediately convert it into a weapon against another child.
“Look at him. Why can you not be like him?”

Uncle, Aunty, with the greatest respect, how much did you score when you were in school? Sixty per cent? Seventy? I genuinely do not know, and I am not going to invent a number just to win an argument. But if your own marks were ordinary, why is your child required to deliver a performance that would make a national topper nervous?
And even if you scored 99.99%, congratulations. Genuinely. But your child is not a sequel to your report card.
Then comes the legendary speech about how difficult education was in your time.
“In our days, papers were so difficult. Nowadays everything is easy. You children are lazy. You have everything available, yet you do not study.”

Uncle, please. You have just spent fifteen minutes forwarding a WhatsApp message claiming that drinking hot water cures every disease known to humanity. Let us not turn this into an international assessment of intellectual competence.

Education has changed. Access to information has changed. Competition has changed. The pressure placed on students has changed. Some things may be easier now, others are considerably harder, and comparing two generations using nothing but personal nostalgia is not a serious analysis of education.
More importantly, even if your generation had the toughest examinations in human history, what exactly does that prove? That the next generation must suffer in the same way?

If you had to walk ten kilometres to school, should your child be forbidden from taking the bus? If you struggled to afford books, should your child be denied a library? If you had no access to counselling, should your child be expected to silently endure a mental-health crisis?
We are supposed to improve the conditions we inherit. Not preserve every hardship as a family tradition.

And please stop using other children as measuring instruments. A child is not a failed version of the neighbour’s child. They are not a percentage with legs. They are a human being who is still figuring out what they are good at, what they care about, and who they want to become.
If Sharmaji ka beta wants to become a doctor, wonderful. If your child wants to become a painter, let us at least have the conversation before declaring the dream dead.

sections.heading: Let Them Fall. Seriously.
paragraphs: One of the most frustrating things about this entire conversation is the way failure is treated as something parents must prevent at any cost.

Parents want their children to succeed, which is understandable. But sometimes, in trying to protect them from every possible mistake, they also protect them from the very experiences that teach them how to make decisions.

Let your child try something and discover that they are not good at it. Let them enter a competition and lose. Let them train for a football match and get knocked out. Let them paint something terrible. Let them write an article nobody reads. Let them start a project that does not work.
Let them experience the uncomfortable realisation that wanting something badly does not automatically make them good at it.
That is not cruelty. That is learning.

A child who fails at something they chose has an opportunity to ask questions. What went wrong? Did I enjoy the process? Do I want to improve? Was I unprepared? Is this still worth pursuing? Should I try a different approach? Or have I discovered that I do not actually want this as much as I thought I did?
These are lessons a child cannot fully learn when every decision is made for them and every failure is treated as a family emergency.

And no, I am not saying parents should let children make every decision without guidance. Children need boundaries, information, support, and adults who can help them recognise genuine risks. Some careers are financially uncertain. Some plans need a backup. Some dreams require years of work and a realistic understanding of the industry.
But guidance should make a child better equipped to choose. It should not quietly remove the choice altogether.

Imagine a child who wants to pursue art. Instead of dismissing the idea, a parent could help them understand the options: fine arts, illustration, animation, design, teaching, commercial work, or combining art with another field. They could discuss money, training, competition, and a practical backup plan without treating the original dream as a joke.

The same applies to sport. Professional football is intensely competitive, and not everyone will make it. That is a legitimate concern. But a child can still explore the sport seriously, understand what it takes, and make informed decisions with support instead of being told that the dream is over before they have properly tested it.
The goal is not to promise success. The goal is to give the child enough room to discover what success might mean to them.

Because there is a particular kind of regret that comes from failing at something you genuinely tried to do. It hurts, but at least you have an answer. You know what happened. You know what you learned. You know that you gave it a chance.
Regret from never trying is different. It leaves a question mark where an experience should have been.
“I tried and failed” is a sentence a person can learn to live with.
“I was never allowed to try” can follow them for years.
And perhaps that is what parents should fear more than a child failing at one dream: a child growing up believing that their own wishes were never important enough to be taken seriously.

sections.heading: 3 Idiots, Taare Zameen Par, Udaan. How Many Times Do We Need to Say This?
paragraphs: We have been talking about this for years. We have made films about it, cried over them, quoted them, recommended them to our friends, and then returned home to continue the same conversations with our own families.

3 Idiots told us that chasing excellence can be more meaningful than chasing a label. Taare Zameen Par reminded us that children learn differently and that a struggling student may need understanding rather than humiliation. Udaan showed us the damage that can happen when a parent’s authority leaves no room for a child’s identity.
Beautiful films. Important messages. Absolute cinema.
And then the credits roll, somebody wipes their tears, and a parent turns to their child and says, “Very nice movie. Now go study for your engineering entrance examination.”
WHAT HAPPENED TO ALL THAT EMOTIONAL GROWTH WE JUST EXPERIENCED FOR TWO HOURS?

Of course, watching a film does not automatically make anyone a better parent. Real life involves financial pressure, uncertainty, family responsibilities, and difficult trade-offs that a two-hour screenplay cannot completely resolve.
But if we can understand the message when it is delivered through a fictional character, why is it so difficult to apply it to our own children?
Why can we applaud a film about allowing a child to discover their strengths, then treat our own child’s different interests as a threat to their future?
Perhaps the problem is not that we do not understand the message. Perhaps understanding it in theory is easier than accepting the uncertainty that comes with actually following it.
It is easy to say every child is different. It is harder when your child is different from the child you imagined.

sections.heading: The Numbers Are Not Just Numbers.
paragraphs: Now, I love statistics. Which is a slightly unfortunate hobby for someone who has also spent a considerable amount of time struggling with mathematics. But numbers have a way of forcing a conversation beyond personal opinions.

According to the National Crime Records Bureau’s Accidental Deaths and Suicides in India 2024 report, India recorded 14,488 student suicides in 2024. That was 596 more than the 13,892 recorded in 2023, an increase of about 4.3%. Student suicides accounted for 8.5% of all recorded suicide deaths that year.
That works out to roughly 40 student deaths by suicide every day.
Read that again. Forty. Every. Day.
The number of student suicides also increased by around 15.7% between 2020 and 2024. Over the decade from 2014 to 2024, the reported count rose from 8,068 to 14,488.

These are recorded deaths, not a complete measure of student distress. And we must be careful not to claim that all of these deaths were caused by parents, exams, or competitive education. Suicide is complex, and the NCRB records multiple reported circumstances and causes.
But the figures should make us ask uncomfortable questions about the environment in which our children are growing up.

The 2024 NCRB data also recorded 11,184 suicides among children below 18. Among the reported causes for this age group, family problems accounted for 3,101 deaths, relationship issues for 1,671, illness for 1,347, and failure in examination for 1,071.
Across student suicides overall, examination failure was attributed in 2,032 cases.

Let me make an important distinction: these figures do not mean that 2,032 children died solely because their parents wanted better marks. They do show that examination failure appears among the reported circumstances of a devastating number of deaths, alongside family problems, illness, and other forms of distress.
The lesson is not that examinations are the only problem. It is that we cannot treat exam pressure as harmless simply because every generation has experienced some version of it.

And the gender figures matter, too. Of the 14,488 student suicides recorded in 2024, 7,669 were male and 6,819 were female. This is not a problem that belongs to one gender. Boys and girls can both suffer under academic expectations, family conflict, and fear of failure.

There is another important limitation: the number of deaths is not the same as a suicide rate per student. To calculate that rate accurately, we would need a reliable denominator for the entire student population, measured consistently. The absolute numbers are still alarming, but we should not pretend they tell us everything.

Behind every figure is a person whose future ended before it could unfold. A person who might have become a teacher, a designer, a parent, a scientist, an artist, or simply someone who eventually figured out what made them happy.
A person who deserved the chance to discover that one examination, one result, or one terrible year was not the entire story of their life.

If you are a student reading this and you feel trapped by marks, family expectations, or a future that seems to have been decided for you, please tell someone you trust. You do not need to wait until things become unbearable to ask for help. In India, Tele-MANAS offers mental-health support at 14416.

Sources: [NCRB 2024 student suicide figures](https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-news/14488-student-deaths-recorded-in-2024-rising-faster-than-overall-rate-ncrb-101778416840680.html), [India Today analysis of child suicide data](https://www.indiatoday.in/education-today/news/story/ncrb-2024-child-suicide-data-exam-failure-family-problems-among-leading-causes-2958266-2026-07-28), and [NCRB data portal](https://ncrb.gov.in/accidental-deaths-suicides-in-india-year-wise.html).

sections.heading: Welcome to the Competitive Exam Hunger Games.
paragraphs: Now let us talk about competitive examinations, because apparently a teenager cannot simply study a subject anymore. They must survive an entire ecosystem built around the possibility that one examination might determine the direction of their life.

JEE. NEET. UPSC, eventually. Entrance tests, cut-offs, coaching institutes, mock examinations, rankings, percentile calculations, and the constant reminder that thousands of other people want the same limited number of seats.

Competition itself is not the villain. Universities and professional courses have limited seats, and some selection process is necessary. The problem is when the entire system becomes so narrow that a student starts believing one unsuccessful attempt means they have failed as a human being.

A study examining media-reported suicides among JEE and NEET aspirants found that 81% of the cases in its sample involved people aged 15–20, 77.2% involved males, and 73.4% involved NEET aspirants. Rajasthan accounted for 69.6% of the reported cases studied.

These were media-reported cases, not a representative sample of every aspirant who struggles. We cannot use them to estimate the percentage of students who will experience suicidal thoughts. But the findings illustrate the seriousness of distress in highly competitive coaching environments.

Another analysis using district-level NCRB data found student suicides rose by 17.5% during NEET-UG or JEE-Mains examination months, with the association stronger for girls and in districts with high participation in competitive examinations. That is an association, not proof that examinations alone caused those deaths, but it is a reason to investigate the pressure surrounding them.
And think about the contradiction. We tell students that education is supposed to open doors, then create a culture where one examination can feel like a door slamming shut forever.

If you do not get the rank, you try again. If you do not get it again, you may spend another year preparing. Your friends move ahead. Your relatives ask questions. Your parents worry about the money spent. Every birthday becomes another reminder that time is passing.

Some students thrive in that environment. Others do not. Some need more time. Some discover a different interest. Some are capable but exhausted. Some are not suited to the course they were trying to enter in the first place.
But the system does not always leave enough room for those differences.

And parents can make it worse when they treat every alternative as an excuse. Taking a different route becomes failure. Choosing another subject becomes wasted potential. Taking a break becomes laziness. Changing direction becomes an embarrassment.
What exactly are we preparing children for if they are never allowed to change direction?

sections.heading: And Then the Papers Leak. Brilliant.
paragraphs: As if the pressure was not enough, we have also managed to make students question whether the examination itself is fair.

Imagine preparing for a competitive exam for two years. Imagine spending your family’s savings on coaching, giving up holidays, missing birthdays, sleeping with a syllabus beside your bed, and calculating your future in mock-test scores.
Then imagine discovering that the paper may have been leaked.
What are you supposed to feel? Anger? Betrayal? Helplessness? All three?

The NEET-UG controversy in 2024 triggered a CBI investigation and Supreme Court proceedings after allegations that examination material had circulated before the test. The UGC-NET examination was cancelled a day after it was held because of concerns about its integrity.

In 2026, NEET-UG faced another major paper-leak scandal. The CBI investigation led to arrests and charges against individuals alleged to have been involved in the leak. The case remained a matter of investigation and legal proceedings, so allegations must not be confused with final convictions.

An investigation by The Indian Express also reported 45 major paper-leak cases over 24 years. That is not a count of every allegation ever made, but it gives an indication of how long examination integrity has been a concern.

Sources: [The Indian Express on paper leaks](https://indianexpress.com/article/education/45-major-paper-leaks-in-24-years-few-top-officials-face-action-10724671/) and [Reuters on the 2026 NEET investigation](https://www.reuters.com/world/india/indian-federal-police-file-charges-against-13-over-exam-paper-leaks-2026-07-30/).
Let us be clear: not every exam allegation is proven, and not every examination is compromised. But even the repeated occurrence of major controversies can damage trust in the system.

For an honest student, the promise of a competitive examination is simple: prepare, perform, and be judged fairly. When that promise is questioned, the student is left wondering whether effort was ever enough.

And that is the cruelest part. Students are told that their future depends on hard work, discipline, and merit. Then they watch scandals that suggest access, corruption, or leaks may interfere with the very process that is supposed to reward them.
We cannot tell a child to trust the system and then act surprised when they begin to doubt it.

If an examination is important enough to influence millions of lives, its security, transparency, and accountability should be treated as essential responsibilities. Encrypted question-paper systems, randomised question banks, strict access controls, independent investigations, and transparent public reporting are not extravagant demands. They are basic requirements for a system asking young people to place their futures in its hands.

sections.heading: The Education System: Are We Learning or Just Collecting Marks?
paragraphs: Here is a question I keep coming back to. What is education actually supposed to do?

Is it supposed to teach a child how to think, ask questions, solve problems, understand the world, communicate, create, and develop the confidence to learn new things? Or is it supposed to produce a percentage that can be compared with the percentage of somebody else’s child?
Because the numbers on foundational learning give us something important to think about.

ASER 2024 found that 23.4% of children in Class 3 attending government schools in rural India could read a Class 2-level text. That was an improvement from 16.3% in 2022, which is genuinely encouraging. Among government-school students in Class 5, 44.8% could read a Class 2-level text, while the figure for Class 8 was 67.5%.
In arithmetic, 33.7% of Class 3 children across schools could solve a basic subtraction problem in 2024, while 45.8% of Class 8 students could perform basic arithmetic as measured by the survey.

These numbers show progress in some areas, especially since the pandemic-era learning setbacks. They also show that foundational learning remains uneven. And ASER is a rural household survey, so these findings should not be presented as a measurement of every child in every Indian school.

Still, consider the contradiction. We ask students to tackle increasingly advanced syllabuses and high-stakes examinations, while a substantial number are still struggling with basic reading and arithmetic.

A child who needs help with reading should receive that help. A child who struggles with mathematics should have the chance to build the foundations properly. They should not be made to feel stupid because the curriculum has moved on without them.
If we only measure whether the syllabus was completed, we may miss whether the student actually understood it.
And if we reward memorising answers more than asking good questions, we should not be surprised when children become excellent at reproducing information but afraid of being wrong.
Mistakes are part of learning. Curiosity requires room to explore. Creativity requires the possibility of producing something that does not work the first time.
Yet too often, the classroom and the home send the opposite message: get the answer right, get the highest marks, and do not give anyone a reason to question your ability.
How do we expect children to become independent thinkers if every wrong answer becomes a personal failure?

sections.heading: Meanwhile, Other Countries Are Doing Things Differently.
paragraphs: Whenever someone criticises Indian education, somebody will inevitably say, “Then go and study in Finland.” I am not suggesting we copy another country wholesale. Education systems operate within different cultures, economies, languages, and social conditions.
But we can learn from what other systems prioritise.

In PISA 2022, Singapore recorded some of the highest scores among participating systems, with an average of 575 in mathematics, 543 in reading, and 561 in science. Finland also performed strongly in several areas. India did not participate in PISA 2022 as a nationally representative system, so it would be misleading to put an Indian national score beside Singapore’s as if both had taken the same assessment under comparable conditions.
India did participate in an earlier PISA exercise in 2009 through selected regions, including Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh, but that is not a substitute for a contemporary national comparison.

What can we learn, then? Not that students in another country have perfect lives or that their systems have no pressure. Singapore, for example, is itself known for demanding academic expectations. The useful question is what strong education systems do to build understanding, support teachers, identify learning gaps, and give students pathways to progress.

The OECD’s research on PISA highlights the importance of strong foundational skills, teacher capacity, and learning environments that help students apply knowledge rather than merely recall it. High-performing systems vary, but they generally have ways to monitor learning and support students who are falling behind.

India has its own reforms and promising initiatives. ASER 2024 shows that foundational learning has improved since 2022. The National Education Policy 2020 also calls for more flexibility, competency-based assessment, vocational education, and reduced dependence on rote learning.

The problem is not that India has no ideas for improving education. The problem is whether those ideas reach classrooms consistently, whether teachers have the resources to implement them, and whether families trust a wider range of educational pathways.
We need to move beyond the assumption that a child’s entire ability can be measured by performance in one high-pressure examination.

A stronger system would identify struggling students earlier, offer remedial support without humiliating them, provide meaningful vocational and academic alternatives, strengthen career counselling, and make mental-health support accessible.

It would allow a student to change interests without feeling that they had destroyed their future. It would help parents understand that a child who is not suited to medicine can still build a meaningful life. And it would measure whether students can use what they learn, not simply whether they can reproduce it under timed conditions.
We do not need to stop valuing academic achievement. We need to stop treating it as the only form of achievement that deserves respect.

Sources: [OECD PISA 2022 results](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/pisa-2022-results-volume-i_53f23881-en/full-report/how-did-countries-perform-in-pisa_dc514907.html), [OECD information on India’s participation](https://www.oecd.org/en/about/programmes/pisa/india.html), and [ASER 2024 findings](https://indianexpress.com/article/education/aser-2024-govt-schools-reading-basic-arithmetic-levels-9803316/).

sections.heading: Dear Parents, Responsibility Is Not the Same as Control.
paragraphs: I know some parents will read this and say, “We only want what is best for our children.” And I believe many of you mean exactly that.

But wanting what is best for a child does not automatically mean knowing what is best for them. Love can coexist with fear. Good intentions can still produce harmful pressure. And a decision made to protect a child can sometimes leave them feeling that they have no control over their own life.
Parents should absolutely discuss money, employment, uncertainty, and the realities of a chosen career. Children deserve honest information, not a fantasy that passion alone guarantees success.

But the conversation should include the child’s interests, strengths, doubts, and willingness to take the risk. It should include backup plans without using those backup plans as a threat. It should allow the child to say, “I understand this is difficult, but I still want to try.”
And parents should be prepared for the possibility that their child’s definition of a good life will not match their own.

Maybe the child will become a doctor. Maybe an engineer. Maybe a painter who eventually makes a living from their work. Maybe a footballer. Maybe someone who starts in one field and changes direction at twenty-five. Maybe someone who never becomes particularly famous or wealthy but finds meaningful work, builds good relationships, and lives with a sense of peace.
None of those futures can be guaranteed in advance.

But a child should not have to earn the right to be loved by meeting a particular academic standard. They should not have to prove their worth with a rank. And they should not be made to feel that a disappointing result has brought shame upon the family.

If your child fails, ask what happened before deciding what it means. If they want to change direction, listen before refusing. If they are struggling, take their distress seriously. If they tell you they are unhappy, do not immediately respond with a lecture about how much harder your own life was.
Your child does not need you to agree with every dream. They need to know that you will take the dream seriously enough to discuss it honestly.
They need to know that if a plan fails, the relationship between you will not fail with it.

Because the purpose of parenting is not to produce a child who follows instructions perfectly. It is to help a young person gradually develop the judgement, resilience, and confidence to make decisions for themselves.
